props.title: An Education
props.initialSlug: Teen's 1960s affair with older man tests her future

sections.content: **An Education** (2009) brilliantly captures the intoxicating allure of sophistication through the eyes of 16-year-old Jenny, played masterfully by Carey Mulligan in her breakthrough role. The film joins other coming-of-age stories like **Notes on a Scandal** (2006) and **The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie** (1969) in exploring how intellectual young women can be drawn into dangerous relationships with seemingly worldly mentors. Set in 1961 London, it shares DNA with **The Graduate** (1967) in examining the seductive pull of adult sophistication, though here the power dynamic is even more troubling.

sections.content: Nick Hornby's screenplay adaptation of Lynn Barber's memoir deftly balances Jenny's intellectual awakening with the darker undertones of manipulation. Like **The Virgin Suicides** (1999) and **American Beauty** (1999), the film examines how teenage girls' coming-of-age stories often intersect dangerously with older men's midlife crises. Peter Sarsgaard's David is particularly chilling in how he weaponizes cultural capital - art, music, literature - as grooming tools.

The film's 1960s setting provides crucial context, with Jenny caught between post-war propriety and the coming sexual revolution. Similar to **Revolutionary Road** (2008) and **Carol** (2015), it explores how bright young women struggled against suffocating social expectations. Alfred Molina and Cara Seymour deliver nuanced performances as Jenny's parents, whose own limited horizons make them vulnerable to David's sophisticated manipulation. SUBHEAD: The Price of Sophistication

sections.content: What sets **An Education** (2009) apart is how it interrogates the very nature of sophistication and cultural knowledge. Like **Dead Poets Society** (1989) and **The History Boys** (2006), it questions what constitutes a real education versus mere performance of intellectualism. Jenny's Oxford aspirations become complicated by David's promises of a different kind of worldly education, one that proves hollow but nonetheless tempting.
